rationale: Start with a broad, relatively strong scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds within 42 min if possible and map the overall retention window. This gives a balanced first read on whether the mixture is compressed early, spread across the run, or at risk of truncation.

The first run shows the mixture is grossly overcompressed at the void, so the next priority is maximum retention and maximum gradient shallowness to spread the early cluster. Use the weakest start, longest gradient, and lowest temperature while keeping a strong final organic to avoid losing late compounds.

Only one adjacent pair is limiting, and the current method is heavily over-resolved elsewhere but pays a large time penalty. Halving the gradient time should substantially improve CRF by pulling t_last down while likely keeping the critical pair near acceptable resolution.

The remaining problem is selectivity, not overall retention, and both critical pairs sit mid-gradient while the last peak still has margin before 42 min. Lowering phi1 should reshape the gradient strength and often changes spacing/selectivity in the middle of the chromatogram without sacrificing observability.

Dropping phi1 to 0.60 improved the 3/4 pair and removed the 6/7 collapse, but cost too much time; this suggests an intermediate phi1 may preserve the selectivity gain with a much smaller time penalty. Testing 0.75 directly maps that tradeoff around the current best tG and T.

The data suggest a selectivity crossover with phi1: low phi1 helps pair 3/4 while high phi1 helps pair 6/7, so the optimum may lie between 0.75 and 0.95. Testing 0.85 should balance both critical pairs while keeping the run shorter than the 0.60 and 0.75 cases.

At phi1 0.95, lengthening the gradient from 20 to 40 min greatly improved pair 3/4 but overpenalized time, so 30 min is the most informative midpoint. It may lift both critical pairs enough to improve the resolution term materially while keeping t_last in a more favorable range than the 40 min run.

Gradient shape alone is not resolving both critical pairs, so probe temperature as the main remaining selectivity lever while keeping the fastest broadly successful gradient framework. A large temperature jump is the most efficient way to test whether either coelution can be broken enough to raise the resolution term without sacrificing too much time.

All pairs are fully resolved at 20 min, so the remaining objective is to shorten the method until a pair drops below 1.5 or t_last moves to 10 min or less. Reducing tG one step to 18 min is the most direct exploitation move around the current best method.

The 18 min run is already near-optimal, but CRF can still improve if t_last drops to 10 min or below and the slight loss in one pair does not outweigh the time gain. One more step shorter is the right boundary test before backing off if resolution falls too far.

The optimum is clearly near 18 min at high temperature, and the limiting pair is 4/5; a small temperature decrease may recover that pair's resolution enough to outweigh any modest time increase. This is a local refinement around the current best method rather than a broader shape change.

Temperature strongly changes selectivity in this system, and the limiting pair switched when dropping from 60 to 55 C. Testing 50 C at the best tG maps whether there is a sharper local optimum in selectivity around high temperature that can beat the current 18 min, 60 C method.

Use the current optimum framework but reduce phi1 one step to 0.90 to probe whether the limiting 4/5 pair gains enough selectivity to offset a small increase in retention. This is the cleanest local adjustment left around the best method without repeating a prior run.

At phi1 0.90 all pairs are fully resolved, so the next step is to shorten the run until the critical pair approaches the threshold. This tests whether the selectivity gain at 0.90 can preserve full resolution at 16 min and beat the current best 18 min, 0.95 method.

Probe phi0 as the remaining local variable around the current optimum: a slightly stronger starting composition may trim retention and potentially bring t_last to 10 min or below without drastically disturbing the already favorable selectivity. This is a focused boundary test near the best-performing region.

Lowering phi1 improved the critical 4/5 pair at 18 min, so combining that selectivity shift with the faster 16 min gradient may land closer to the optimum balance than either 16/0.95 or 18/0.90. This is the most promising unexplored local combination around the current best region.

Current best performance is on the edge of the time threshold with only a slight resolution deficit in one pair, so one more shortening test is justified if paired with phi1 0.90, which previously improved that critical pair. This checks whether a shorter gradient can still keep the worst pair near 1.5 while dropping t_last further below 10 min.

The 16 min and 18 min results at high temperature suggest the optimum lies on a narrow ridge where pair 4/5 hovers near the 1.5 threshold and t_last is just above 10 min. Running 18 min at phi1 0.85 tests whether the lower final strength can preserve the same near-threshold resolution while slightly shifting retention enough to break the current tie at the top.

Since 16 min is close to optimal on time but pair 4/5 is slightly underresolved, step phi1 down once more from 0.85 to 0.80 to test whether that pair gains enough selectivity to offset any modest retention increase. This is a focused local search around the top-performing region without repeating prior conditions.

At phi1 0.80 the critical pair is fully resolved but t_last is too long; shortening to 14 min directly tests whether that extra selectivity margin can be traded for enough speed to surpass the current best. This is the most plausible remaining way to improve CRF without changing the favorable high-temperature selectivity.

The pattern suggests pair 4/5 improves as phi1 decreases, but time worsens; 0.80/16 was fully resolved but just too slow. Testing 0.75/16 checks whether a further selectivity gain can be achieved with only a small time increase, potentially revealing whether the CRF ridge is broad enough to support a better compromise.

We have mapped a clear phi1–time tradeoff ridge, and 0.80/14 came close; testing 0.70/14 extends that trend to see whether additional selectivity gain can compensate at all or confirm the optimum has already been passed. With only a few injections left, this helps close off the remaining plausible low-phi1 corner near the best region.

The low-phi1 region consistently gives full resolution but incurs a time penalty; shortening further is the only way it could still beat the current best. A 12 min gradient at phi1 0.60 tests the remaining plausible corner where stronger compression of overall run time might offset the added retention while keeping the formerly critical pair above threshold.

Most unexplored gains are exhausted around phi1 and tG, so use one of the last injections to test whether a slightly lower temperature on a somewhat longer gradient can restore full resolution while keeping t_last close enough to 10 min to challenge the current best. This probes a nearby ridge suggested by the strong selectivity sensitivity to temperature.

For the last shot, test the strongest remaining selectivity shift in the successful high-temperature region while keeping a short gradient to control the time term. The search indicates the optimum is a narrow tradeoff near full resolution and t_last about 10 min; this unexplored extreme low-phi1 point is the only remaining chance to beat the current tie by changing the critical-pair spacing more than the time penalty.
